title: A Name
gist: A note on the quiet privilege of belonging to a family name, and on building one worth giving.
body:
A note to anyone who has never had to think about theirs.

You probably don't remember the first time someone asked whose child you were. Why would you? It wasn't a question that required thought. You answered the way you'd answer if someone asked whether you had a nose — without pause, without hesitation. I'm a Kayonga. A Bunyenyezi. A Kayoboke. The name arrived before the words did, before the room did, before you did, almost. Your parents gave it to you the way they gave you a roof — not as a gift exactly. More as an unconscious responsibility.

I've been thinking about that. Quite a lot, actually.

I had light banter with Joanita earlier today and found myself startled mid-conversation. Kayonga — just a name to her, but an identity from where I stood. Be it in how she introduced herself, the surname doing quiet work the first name never could. Be it in how she'd point casually across a room — he's one of us, the us in that sentence carrying the full weight of a family, a reputation, a belonging she'd never had to earn.

How significant it is to belong. To be part of something larger than yourself. And yet the way it happens — the sheer, unbothered ease of it — means it can become so unremarkable that you deploy it like punctuation, without weight, without ceremony, without once pausing to consider what it would cost not to have it.

You can say my sibling and own them. Completely, confidently, without footnote. Your parents did that. They created a web — and in each thread, ingrained before you were old enough to understand what a name carries, an identity. To be a Karuletwa, a Kayonga, a Bunyenyezi — whatever name your people carried before you arrived. You do not walk into rooms alone. You walk in trailing a history that arrived before you and will outlast you, and you've been doing it so long it feels unremarkable.

There is a question people ask here — uriwakwande? Whose are you? Where do you come from? It sounds simple. It is not simple. It is the oldest form of identification there is. And if you know the answer without hesitation, if the name rises in your throat the way your first language does — before thought, before effort — ndi wa kwa Kayonga — then you are holding something rarer than you know. The room shifts when a name like that lands. Not always visibly. But it shifts.

Your parents gave you pedigree. Character you didn't have to build from scratch. Unpaid gratitude you get to collect on. Respect that walked into the room ahead of you. You have a debit card you didn't earn and have been spending since birth. And here is the part that really caught me — it's not even yours to keep. Think about it. To be a Karuletwa means your kids, your siblings, your mother, your father's father — they all hold the same name, the same thread. One day your children will cash out on it. Their heads will be held at a height partly determined by how well you nourished what was handed to you. The name travels. It compounds. It is, in the truest sense, a legacy already in motion before you arrived.

That is not a small thing. It is an enormous thing dressed in the ordinary clothes of something everyone around you also has — so you've never had reason to look at it twice.

Aho ubaririzgwa.

A lineage. A web. A room you were born already inside of.

Some of us are still looking for the door.

Not to be a cliché, but it got me thinking about scripture. John 14:13 — whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son — the name is not decorative. It carries weight, and what you do inside it either honours or diminishes whose you are. And Psalm 2:7-8, where God turns to his son and declares you are my Son; today I have begotten you — the sonship is declared first. The inheritance follows the identity, not the other way around. You are named, therefore you belong. You belong, therefore you may ask. You may ask, therefore you are expected to show up as someone who knows it.

Which made me wonder, quietly, whether I have failed my own legacy. Not the family name — but that one. If I truly understood the weight of what it meant to be God's child, would I not show up more boldly? More confidently? With more authority and less second-guessing? I wander off in thought on this — it is perhaps too large a question for one sitting — but it was simply the closest association I could make. The names we are given before we understand them. The lives we are asked to live up to. The gap, always, between whose we are and how we actually walk.

I want to be clear — I write this not with bitterness. The envy I hold on your behalf is the generous kind, the kind that looks at something beautiful and wants you to see it too, because you're standing so close you've gone a little blind to it. That's the thing about ordinary miracles. They stop looking like miracles.

And then there is the quiet reckoning I haven't said out loud until now. To give my own children the same foundation, I would have to marry into a name. Ironical, ancient, and more true than most people with modern sensibilities would like to admit. It is a path. Perhaps the easier one. But I keep turning over the other possibility — quieter, longer, built on deliberate intention rather than inheritance — that I may just have my one little one, and live so fully, so honestly, so purposefully, that one day they walk into a room and say it without rehearsal: ndi wa kwa Kayitesi. A name they didn't inherit. One we built, thread by thread.

Either way — what a privilege it is. To have a name. To give one. To become one worth giving.

So in case no one has said it plainly: you are extremely lucky. And the least you can do with that luck is know it.
